column1: What is a measure, in one line?
column2: A rule that gives sets a size from 0 to infinity, with size 0 for the empty set and sizes adding over countably many disjoint sets.
Each point weighs 1. The size of a set is the number of its points.
A set of measure 0, such as any countable set of points on the line.

column1: Why do the rationals in \( [0,1] \) have length 0?
column2: Cover the k-th rational with an interval of length \( \varepsilon/2^k \). The total is at most \( \varepsilon \), for any \( \varepsilon > 0 \).
The infimum of the total length of countable interval covers of \( E \).

column1: What does the Vitali set show?
column2: With the axiom of choice, some sets have no length that is both additive and unchanged by sliding.
Contains the whole space, closed under complements, closed under countable unions.

column1: What is Lebesgue measure on the line?
column2: The measure that gives every interval its length and does not change when a set slides.
When every set \( \{x : f(x) > t\} \) is measurable.

column1: Integral of a simple function \( \sum c_k \mathbf{1}_{A_k} \)?
column2: \( \sum c_k \mu(A_k) \): value times measure, added up.

column1: Riemann versus Lebesgue in the coin picture?
column2: Riemann adds coins one by one in order. Lebesgue sorts by value, counts each pile, multiplies and adds.

column1: Lebesgue integral of the Dirichlet function on \( [0,1] \)?
column2: 0. Value 1 sits on the rationals, a set of measure 0. Riemann fails on this function.
If \( f_n \to f \) pointwise and \( |f_n| \le g \) with \( \int g < \infty \), then \( \int f_n \to \int f \).
